  and id headers, and a body given as `bodyStructure` or as `textBody`,
  `htmlBody` and `attachments`. A part's content is a `bodyValues` entry or a
  `blobId`. `Date` and `Message-ID` are added when not given.
- **update** sets `keywords`, whole or one at a time (`keywords/$seen`), and
  `mailboxIds`, whole or one at a time (`mailboxIds/<id>`). Moving keeps the
  Email's id. A message is never left in no mailbox.
- **destroy** removes the Email from every mailbox it is in.

A move does not count against the quota; a copy into another mailbox does. Each
object fails on its own: one refused id does not fail the rest of the call.

## Changing mailboxes

`Mailbox/set` (RFC 8621 §2.5) creates, renames, moves and destroys mailboxes.
Names are checked as IMAP `CREATE` checks them, and `isSubscribed` writes the
subscription list IMAP reads.

| Refusal | When |
|:---|:---|
| `alreadyExists` | the name is taken |
| `forbidden` | renaming or destroying INBOX |
| `mailboxHasChild` | destroying a mailbox with children |
| `mailboxHasEmail` | destroying a mailbox with mail, without `onDestroyRemoveEmails` |
| `overQuota` | `quota_mailbox_count` is reached |

A renamed mailbox keeps its id and its access rights.

---

## Capabilities

| Capability | RFC | State |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Core — session | RFC 8620 §2 | served |
| Core — request envelope, back-references, `Core/echo` | RFC 8620 §3–§4 | served |
| Mail — `Mailbox/get`, `Mailbox/query`, `Mailbox/set` | RFC 8621 §2 | served |
| Mail — `Email/get` (envelope, bodies, preview) | RFC 8621 §4 | served |
| Mail — `Email/query` (index and full-text conditions) | RFC 8621 §4.4 | served |
| Core — blob upload and download | RFC 8620 §6 | served |
| Mail — `Email/import` | RFC 8621 §4.8 | served |
| Mail — `SearchSnippet/get` | RFC 8621 §5 | served |
| Mail — `Thread/get`, `Thread/changes` | RFC 8621 §3 | served from the account's threading state; a merge is reported in `Email/changes` as well, since a client groups by the `threadId` it holds |
| Mail — `Mailbox/changes` | RFC 8621 §2 | served |
| Mail — `Email/changes` | RFC 8621 §4 | served |
| Mail — `Mailbox/queryChanges`, `Email/queryChanges` | RFC 8620 §5.6 | registered; answers `cannotCalculateChanges` |
| Mail — `Email/set` | RFC 8621 §4.6 | served: create, keywords, `mailboxIds`, destroy |
| Quota — `Quota/get`, `Quota/changes`, `Quota/query`, `Quota/queryChanges` | RFC 9425 | served, read-only |
| Sieve — `SieveScript/get`, `/set`, `/query`, `/validate` | RFC 9661 | served |
| Vacation — `VacationResponse/get`, `/set` | RFC 8621 §8 | served with Sieve scripts when `sieve_vacation_enabled` is on and `sieve_extensions` allows `vacation` |
| Submission — `Identity/get`, `/changes`, `/set`; `EmailSubmission/get`, `/changes`, `/query`, `/queryChanges`, `/set` | RFC 8621 §6–§7 | served when a relay is configured; identities read-only |
| Push over EventSource | RFC 8620 §7.3 | served; see [Push](#push) |
| JMAP over WebSocket, with push | RFC 8887 | served; see [WebSocket](#websocket) |
| Push subscriptions (Web Push) | RFC 8620 §7.2 | not implemented |

The protocol layer lives in `pkg/jmapcore`, which imports nothing from yarilo
and is meant to be extracted as a standalone library.

## Push

`GET /jmap/eventsource/` streams `StateChange` events (RFC 8620 §7.3). It is
the `eventSourceUrl` of the session resource and passes through
`yarilo-jmap-login`.

### Stream parameters

| Parameter | Values |
|:---|:---|
| `types` | type names, comma-separated, or `*` |
| `closeafter` | `state` or `no` |
| `ping` | seconds; `0` sends none |

`*` means every type the server answers: `Email`, `Mailbox`, `Thread` and
`Quota`, plus `Identity`, `EmailSubmission`, `SieveScript` and
`VacationResponse` where they are served. An unknown name is left out, and a
request naming no known type is answered `204`.

`closeafter=state` ends the stream after the first `state` event. A `ping`
event carries `{"interval":N}`.

### Resuming after a disconnect

A `state` event carries the types whose state moved, with their new state
strings, and an `id`. The id is a sequence of the pod that serves the stream;
it means nothing on another pod.

To resume, reconnect with `Last-Event-ID` set to the last id received. Whatever
its value, the current state of every requested type is sent at once, so nothing is missed
while the client was away, even if the account moved to another backend
meanwhile.

Without `Last-Event-ID` the stream starts from the current state and sends
only later changes.

### What moves a type

Every write announces itself through `yarilo-locks`, whatever the protocol
made it, and every pod with an open stream for the account hears it at once.
A stream recomputes only the types the write can move and sends those whose
state changed:

| Write | Types |
|:---|:---|
| a message or its flags: delivery, `APPEND`, `STORE`, copy, move, expunge | `Email`, `Thread`, `Mailbox`, `Quota` |
| a folder created, renamed or deleted; a subscription; a special-use role; an ACL change | `Mailbox` |
| a Sieve script, including the vacation script | `SieveScript`, `VacationResponse` |
| a new conversation in the threading state | `Thread` |
| an `EmailSubmission` record kept or dropped | `EmailSubmission` |

`jmap_push_poll` is a safety net under the events: every that many seconds a
stream recomputes all its types, which catches a write made while the pod had
lost its channel to `yarilo-locks`. A lost channel is asked for again every
two seconds, and once it is back every type is recomputed. With
`jmap_push_poll: 0` the endpoint answers `204`.

`Identity` is read from userdb and has no write path in Yarilo. It moves only
when userdb does, which no event announces; the recompute picks it up.

### Kicks

The stream outlives the proxy's request timeouts, and a kick ends it: a
session kick from the admin API, or a director `USER-KICKED` for the user,
including a move to another backend. The client reconnects with
`Last-Event-ID` and reaches the user's new backend.

## WebSocket

`GET /jmap/ws/` upgrades to JMAP over WebSocket (RFC 8887). The session
resource advertises it as `urn:ietf:params:jmap:websocket`:

```json
{
  "url": "wss://mail.example.com/jmap/ws/",
  "supportsPush": true
}
```

- `url` is `jmap_base_url` with `https` turned into `wss`.
- `supportsPush` is false when `jmap_push_poll` is `0`.
- With `jmap_websocket_timeout: 0` the capability is not advertised and the
  endpoint answers `404`.

The client must offer the `jmap` subprotocol in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`;
without it the upgrade is refused with `400`. The connection authenticates
like any other request to `yarilo-jmap-login`, and browser origins are
checked against `jmap_cors_allow_origins` before the upgrade.

### Requests

A text message whose `@type` is `Request` is an API request. It runs exactly as
a `POST` to the API endpoint, with the same limits. Requests on one connection
are answered in order:

- `Response` carries the method responses, `sessionState` and, when the
  request had an `id`, `requestId`.
- `RequestError` replaces it when the request is refused, with `type`,
  `status`, `detail` and `requestId`.

A message over `maxSizeRequest` is answered with a `limit` `RequestError`, and
a message that is not JSON or has an unknown `@type` with `notJSON` or
`notRequest`. The connection stays open after each. A binary message closes
it with code `1003`.

### Push over WebSocket

Turn push on for a connection, for some types or for all with `null`:

```json
{"@type": "WebSocketPushEnable", "dataTypes": ["Email", "Mailbox"]}
```

From then on the server sends a `StateChange` whenever one of those types
moves, from the same events as EventSource (see [What moves a
type](#what-moves-a-type)):

```json
{
  "@type": "StateChange",
  "changed": {"aYWxpY2VAZXhhbXBsZS5jb20": {"Email": "s42"}},
  "pushState": "eyJFbWFpbCI6InM0MiJ9"
}
```

- A new `WebSocketPushEnable` replaces the earlier one;
  `WebSocketPushDisable` stops it.
- The enable is in place before the next message on the connection is
  handled. A change the client makes in a request sent after the enable is
  always pushed.
- With `jmap_push_poll: 0` both messages are refused as an unknown `@type`.

### Resuming with pushState

`pushState` names the states the connection has been sent. To resume after a
disconnect, send it back in the enable:

```json
{"@type": "WebSocketPushEnable", "dataTypes": ["Email"], "pushState": "eyJFbWFpbCI6InM0MiJ9"}
```

Every requested type whose state moved since is sent at once, in one
`StateChange`, and later changes follow. The server keeps nothing for it, so
the connection can resume on any backend, after a move as well. Without a
`pushState`, or with one that does not decode, push starts from the current
states.

### Idle connections

The server pings every half `jmap_websocket_timeout` and closes a connection
whose client has not answered by the next ping. A client that is alive keeps
its connection, even when it only listens; a browser answers pings on its own.

A kick ends the connection as it ends an EventSource stream, and so does the
server shutting down, with code `1001`. The client reconnects and resumes with
its last `pushState`.

## Quota

`urn:ietf:params:jmap:quota` (RFC 9425) is advertised in the session resource
and per account. A client that speaks only JMAP can read the limit it is being
enforced against, which it previously could not.

One account is one quota root, and the objects are read-only: limits come from
the userdb, not from the client.

| Object | Reported when |
|:---|:---|
| `resourceType: "octets"` | a storage limit is set for the account |
| `resourceType: "count"` | a message-count limit is set (`quota_messages`) |

Both carry `scope: "account"`, `types: ["Mail"]` and the root name
`quota_name` gives IMAP. `hardLimit` is the limit **after** the site-wide
scaling (`quota_storage_percentage`, `quota_storage_extra`), so it is the number
a save is actually judged against, and `warnLimit` is the nearest configured
`quota_warning` threshold below it.

Nothing is reported when the quota engine is off, when `quota_hidden` is set, or
when the user has no limits and `quota_ignore_unlimited` is set — the same three
gates IMAP `GETQUOTA` answers on. A limit nobody enforces is not announced.

`used` is the same count `GETQUOTA` reports, from the same sweep of the
account's folders: two accountings would be two answers to one question. The
units differ because the protocols do — RFC 9208 counts kibibytes, RFC 9425
octets — and the smoke check converts one to the other rather than tolerating a
difference.

### State and changes

The state string carries the numbers themselves, so `Quota/changes` says which
root moved by comparing the state a client holds against the current one, with
no per-client history kept on the server. A state this server did not issue is
answered with `cannotCalculateChanges`, which sends the client back to
`Quota/get`.

`Quota/queryChanges` answers for real, unlike the Mailbox and Email ones, which
are registered and answer `cannotCalculateChanges`: this result set is the
account's own roots, which the state already names, so there is no previous
result to remember.

## Sieve scripts

`urn:ietf:params:jmap:sieve` (RFC 9661) manages the same scripts as
[ManageSieve](/features/sieve#managesieve). Both protocols read and write one store, so
a script uploaded over JMAP is listed by `LISTSCRIPTS` at once, and the reverse.

To store a script, upload its text as a blob, then create it from that blob:

```json
["SieveScript/set", {
  "accountId": "aYWxpY2VAZXhhbXBsZS5jb20",
  "create": {"c1": {"name": "filters", "blobId": "U…"}},
  "onSuccessActivateScript": "#c1"
}, "0"]
```

- The script is checked with the parser and the `sieve_extensions` list that `PUTSCRIPT` uses. A script that does not parse, uses an extension not allowed, or is not UTF-8 gets `invalidSieve`.
- The created script's `blobId` names its stored text. Download it from `downloadUrl`, as `GETSCRIPT` would.
- A create without a name gets one from the server, returned in `created`.
- A create or rename onto a name the account already has gets `alreadyExists` with `existingId`, decided under the store's lock, so a concurrent ManageSieve session cannot be overwritten. An update that renames and replaces the content renames first: a refused name changes nothing.

### Limits

The account capability carries the [`sieve:` section](/features/sieve) limits that ManageSieve enforces:

| Capability field | Key |
|:---|:---|
| `maxSizeScript` | `sieve_max_script_size` |
| `maxNumberScripts` | `sieve_max_num_scripts` |
| `maxNumberRedirects` | `sieve_max_redirects` |
| `sieveExtensions` | `sieve_extensions` |

A limit set to `0` is sent as `null`, no limit. `notificationMethods` is `["mailto"]` while `enotify` is allowed; `externalLists` is `null`.

A script over `sieve_max_script_size` gets `tooLarge`. A new script past `sieve_max_num_scripts`, or one that would take the user's scripts past `sieve_max_storage`, gets `overQuota`. A replaced script is charged for its new size only.

`maxSizeScriptName` is 512 octets, the RFC's floor. A name also stays within the ManageSieve limit of 256 characters, so a name of 257 to 512 one-byte characters is refused although it fits the advertised octets.

### Activation and state

`onSuccessDeactivateScript` runs before `onSuccessActivateScript`, and both only when every create, update and destroy in the call succeeded. The active script cannot be destroyed (`sieveIsActive`); deactivate it in an earlier call.

A script's `id` is kept across a rename. The state string is a counter that every change moves, through either protocol, so `ifInState` and `oldState`/`newState` see a ManageSieve change. RFC 9661 defines no `SieveScript/changes`, so none is served.

A script written to the store behind both protocols, such as a file placed in the home directory, gets an id and moves the state the next time the list is read.

## Vacation response

`VacationResponse` (RFC 8621 §8) is a Sieve script under the hood, managed for the account: `urn:ietf:params:jmap:vacationresponse`, in the same store as the scripts of ManageSieve and `SieveScript`. ManageSieve lists it like any other script.

The script carries the object in a header comment, and below it the rule the object stands for:

- `isEnabled` is a test the rule starts with;
- `fromDate` and `toDate` bound it with `currentdate` (they need `date` and `relational` among `sieve_extensions`, when that list is set);
- `subject` is the reply's subject; one with a control character, a line break included, is refused;
- `textBody` and `htmlBody` are its body. With `htmlBody`, the reply is `multipart/alternative`, and its text part is `textBody` or, when that is null, the text of `htmlBody`. With neither, a default message is sent.

The reply itself is sent as for any Sieve `vacation`; see [Sieve](/features/sieve#vacation-replies).

### When it is enabled

A response is enabled when its `isEnabled` is true and the script runs. The script runs either when it is the account's active script, or when the active script includes it at its top level:

```sieve
require "include";
include :personal "urn:ietf:params:jmap:vacationresponse";
# the rest of the user's own rules
```

`VacationResponse/set` with `isEnabled: true` behaves by what is active:

- **No script is active:** the managed script becomes the active one.
- **The active script already includes the managed one:** nothing else changes.
- **The user's own script is active and does not include it:** the update is refused with `forbidden`. The user's script is never deactivated to make room; add the `include` line above to it, through ManageSieve or `SieveScript/set`, and enable again.

`get` answers `isEnabled: false` whenever the script does not run, whatever was set: for instance after another script was activated through ManageSieve.

### Edited by hand

The managed script can be read and changed through ManageSieve, as any script. If its header comment is missing or no longer parses, `get` answers a response that was never set (disabled, every property null), and the next `set` writes the script anew from what it is given.

The one object's id is `singleton`. `create` and `destroy` answer `singleton` (§8).

## Sending mail

`urn:ietf:params:jmap:submission` is advertised only when `submission_relay_host` is set. Mail goes the way [Submission](/protocols/submission) sends it: the same relay, the same login as the user, the same `submission_max_mail_size` and `submission_max_recipients`.

### Identities

The account's identities are its login, when it is an address, then the userdb field `identity_aliases`, each once whatever its case. They are read-only: `Identity/set` refuses every object with `forbidden`. An identity's `id` is fixed by its address, so a client may keep it.

### Sending a draft

Create an `EmailSubmission` naming an identity and an Email:

```json
["EmailSubmission/set", {
  "accountId": "aYWxpY2VAZXhhbXBsZS5jb20",
  "create": {"s1": {"identityId": "I…", "emailId": "M…"}},
  "onSuccessUpdateEmail": {"#s1": {"keywords/$draft": null}}
}, "0"]
```

The draft can be created in the same request, by an `Email/set` call before this one, and named as `"emailId": "#<its creation id>"`.

- Without an `envelope`, the sender is the address in the last `Sender` header, else in `From`, and the recipients are `To`, `Cc` and `Bcc` without repeats. A sender the identity does not allow is replaced by the identity's address.
- The `From` header must be the identity's address (`forbiddenFrom`); a given `envelope.mailFrom` must be too (`forbiddenMailFrom`). Envelope parameters other than `SIZE` are refused.
- The `Bcc` header is removed before sending, and a `Received` header with `with HTTP` is added when `submission_add_received_header` is on.
- The message is sent at once: `undoStatus` is `final`, `maxDelayedSend` is `0`, and cancelling answers `cannotUnsend`.
- `onSuccessUpdateEmail` and `onSuccessDestroyEmail` run one `Email/set`, whose response comes right after the `EmailSubmission/set` one.

A refusal by the relay that is final (5xx) answers `forbiddenToSend` with the relay's reply. A temporary one (4xx, a relay that does not answer) fails the whole call with `serverFail` while nothing in the call has been sent yet, so the client sends again later. Once a message of the call has gone out, the sent ones are reported in `created` as usual, and the one the relay refused, with every one after it, comes back in `notCreated` with type `serverFail`: retry those, not the whole call.

### Records

`EmailSubmission/get` and `/query` read the records of what was sent, kept `jmap_submission_ttl_seconds` (default 86400) in the user's control directory and dropped when older. `0` keeps none: mail is still sent, and `get` finds nothing. Destroying a record does not touch the mail.

### Limits

Sending over JMAP is held to the same per-user-and-address connection limit as every protocol: `yarilo-jmap-login` counts each connection against `mail_max_userip_connections`, as `yarilo-submission-login` does for SMTP.

---

## Smoke check

```sh
smoketest -host mail.example.com -jmap -jmap-user u1@example.com -jmap-pass secret
```

The checks:

1. an anonymous request is refused with `401`;
2. an authenticated one returns a session resource carrying `capabilities`;
3. a batch of two `Core/echo` calls runs, the second reading the first's result
   through a back-reference;
4. a body one byte over `jmap_max_size_request` is refused by the login layer
   with a `limit` problem;
5. `Mailbox/get` returns a mailbox carrying the `inbox` role, with unique ids
   and every `parentId` naming a mailbox in the same response;
6. `Mailbox/query` filtered by `role:inbox` matches exactly one mailbox, says
   `canCalculateChanges: false`, and a back-referenced `Mailbox/get` in the same
   batch resolves to that mailbox;
7. `Email/query` finds an id, a back-referenced `Email/get` reads it, and the
   blob it names downloads as a non-empty `application/octet-stream`;
8. a download for another account's blob is refused with `404`;
9. a delivered message is found by a `text` condition and read back, and a
   marker that was never delivered finds nothing — the second half is what
   makes the first mean the condition was applied;
10. a round trip through a JMAP client library: a message is uploaded and
    imported, marked read, moved to a new mailbox and destroyed, and a second
    client sees each step in `Email/changes`.

Check 7 needs at least one message in the account. Check 9 needs `-fts-user`,
which states that full-text search is configured, and delivery flags —
`-delivery-host`, `-delivery-port`, `-delivery-proto`; see
[Testing](/operations/testing).

Check 4 sends `-jmap-max-size-request` + 1 bytes; pass the deployment's own
value if it differs from the 10M default.

---

<!-- source: https://doc.yarilomail.org/main/protocols/lmtp.html -->

# LMTP configuration

LMTP (RFC 2033) is the Local Mail Transfer Protocol used for final delivery from an external MTA (Postfix, Exim, etc.) into the yarilo mailbox. It operates on port 24 and returns per-recipient status codes, making it a drop-in replacement for SMTP-based local delivery.

## Architecture

yarilo's LMTP stack is split into two components:

| Binary | Role |
|:---|:---|
| `yarilo-lmtp-login` | MTA-facing proxy. Accepts one LMTP session from the MTA, tracks each recipient in warden (`CONNECT`), issues a service-scoped SESSION token per recipient via yarilo-auth master protocol, then at DATA time fans out one preamble TCP connection to `yarilo-lmtp` per recipient. |
| `yarilo-lmtp` | Backend delivery. Accepts preamble connections (`YARILO\t...TOKEN=...\n`), verifies the token with yarilo-auth (`VERIFY`, `service=lmtp` enforced), and delivers to the mailbox. No XCLIENT, no HAProxy, no direct warden access. |

**Why fan-out?** Each recipient may hash to a different backend pod (in director mode). A single multi-recipient DATA payload is split per recipient so each backend receives exactly the messages it is responsible for. Per-recipient status codes are merged and returned to the MTA.

**Token scoping.** SESSION tokens are issued with `service=lmtp`. The `yarilo-lmtp` `PreambleListener` rejects tokens issued for any other service (imap, pop3, submission), preventing cross-service replay.

See [Services configuration](/architecture/services) for listener-level settings (`port`, `ssl_mode`).

---

## `protocol.lmtp`

### `login_greeting`

- Default: `Yarilo ready.`
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.login_greeting`

Text appended to the `220` banner.

### `lmtp_add_received_header`

- Default: `true`
- Type: boolean
- Also accepted as: `add_received_header`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.add_received_header`

Prepend a `Received:` header to every delivered message.

### `lmtp_save_to_detail_mailbox`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Also accepted as: `save_to_detail_mailbox`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.save_to_detail_mailbox`

Deliver `user+folder@domain` to the `folder` mailbox instead of `INBOX`.

### `lda_mailbox_autocreate`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.lda_mailbox_autocreate`
- See also: `lda_mailbox_autosubscribe`

A delivery to a folder that does not exist creates it. Off, the message
goes to the detail mailbox if that exists, otherwise to `INBOX`.

### `lda_mailbox_autosubscribe`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.lda_mailbox_autosubscribe`
- See also: `lda_mailbox_autocreate`

Subscribe a folder that `lda_mailbox_autocreate` made. Without
`lda_mailbox_autocreate` it does nothing, and startup refuses it.

### `lmtp_verbose_replies`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Also accepted as: `verbose_replies`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.verbose_replies`

Include diagnostic details in `4xx` and `5xx` replies. Useful for
debugging; leave it off in production.

### `lmtp_user_concurrency_limit`

- Default: `10`
- Type: integer
- Also accepted as: `user_concurrency_limit`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.user_concurrency_limit`

Concurrent deliveries per user, counted across the cluster through
yarilo-warden and enforced by yarilo-lmtp-login at `RCPT TO`. Past it the
recipient gets `451 4.3.0` and the MTA retries. `-1` is unlimited; `0`
refuses startup. With warden unreachable a delivery is accepted without
the limit and a warning is logged.

### `lmtp_max_recipients`

- Default: `0`
- Type: integer
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.lmtp_max_recipients`

Recipients per transaction, on the backend and in yarilo-lmtp-login,
advertised as `LIMITS RCPTMAX=N`. The next `RCPT` gets `452 4.5.3`, and
the MTA sends the rest in another transaction. `0` is unlimited.

### `read_timeout`

- Default: `300`
- Type: integer, seconds
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.read_timeout`

Read timeout per command.

### `write_timeout`

- Default: `300`
- Type: integer, seconds
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.write_timeout`

Write timeout per command.


The backend's listen address and port are listener settings (`services.lmtp`, see
[Services](/architecture/services)); the port the login service dials is
`lmtp_login_service.backend_port` below.

### A delivery to a folder that does not exist

A folder a delivery names (`user+folder@` with `lmtp_save_to_detail_mailbox`, or
a Sieve `fileinto`) may not exist yet:

- if a namespace configures it with `auto` (see
  [Namespaces](/storage/namespace#configured-mailboxes-mailboxes)), the delivery
  makes it like any other open, subscribed when `auto: subscribe`. The two
  knobs below play no part in that;
- otherwise, with `lda_mailbox_autocreate: true`, the delivery makes it, and
  subscribes it with `lda_mailbox_autosubscribe: true`;
- otherwise the message goes to the detail mailbox when that is another folder
  and exists, then to `INBOX`. The delivery is not refused.

`fileinto :create` makes the folder regardless of these settings.

### Synthesised Message-ID

#### `lmtp_add_message_id`

- Default: `true`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.add_message_id`

Synthesise a `Message-ID:` when a message arrives without one. An
existing header is never rewritten.


A message stored without a `Message-ID` cannot be replied to and cannot be
threaded, and that is permanent: the header is part of the stored bytes, so
nothing can add it afterwards without rewriting mail. Such a message is its own
root in every conversation, no later reply can name it in `In-Reply-To` or
`References`, and JMAP reports its `messageId` as `null`.

Behind an MTA the header is already present and this key changes nothing. Fed
LMTP directly — a script, or a deployment with no MTA in front — delivery is the
last place the identity can still be given, which is why the default is `true`.
Set it to `false` if the stored bytes must be exactly what arrived.

The identifier is 128 bits of randomness at the server's hostname:

```
Message-ID: <9f0c6a1d4b2e8735c1a0d6f4e2b98357@mx.example.com>
```

Unique among all messages, as RFC 5322 §3.6.4 requires, rather than unique
within one host or one run.

**An existing `Message-ID` is never rewritten**, not even a malformed one:
whatever a sender wrote is what a reply quotes back in `References`, so
replacing it would break the conversation the message already belongs to. Only a
message whose header section has no `Message-ID` field at all is given one — a
header inside a forwarded or quoted message is body, and does not count.

The header is added before Sieve runs, before the message is stored and before
the conversation is recorded, so a script, the stored bytes and the thread all
see the same identity.

```yaml
protocol:
  lmtp:
    login_greeting: "Yarilo ready."
    lmtp_add_received_header: true
    lmtp_add_message_id: true
    lmtp_save_to_detail_mailbox: false
    lmtp_hdr_delivery_address: final
    lmtp_verbose_replies: false
    lmtp_user_concurrency_limit: 5
    read_timeout: 300
    write_timeout: 300
```

---

## Message size and a full mailbox

**Size.** When `quota.quota_mail_size` is set, both `yarilo-lmtp-login` and the
backend LMTP service offer it in the `LHLO` reply as `SIZE <bytes>`:

- `MAIL FROM:<...> SIZE=<n>` above the limit is refused at once with `552`.
- A body that grows past the limit is refused with `552 5.3.4 Maximum message
  size exceeded` while it is being read. The rest is read and discarded rather
  than held in memory, and the connection stays open for the next transaction.

Leave `quota_mail_size` empty or `0` for no limit; then `LHLO` offers a bare
`SIZE` with no number, which RFC 1870 reads as "supported, no fixed limit".

**Full mailbox.** A recipient over quota is answered after `DATA`, with the text
of `quota.quota_exceeded_message`:

| `quota_full_tempfail` | Reply | What the MTA does |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `false` (default) | `552 5.2.2` | Bounces the message to the sender at once. |
| `true` | `452 4.2.2` | Keeps the message queued and retries until the mailbox has room or the queue lifetime runs out. |

Turn it on only when a full mailbox is expected to be emptied soon and a
delayed message is better than a bounce. Otherwise the sender learns of the
failure only when the MTA gives up, often days later.

### `quota_full_tempfail`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.quota_full_tempfail`

Reply for a recipient whose mailbox is full: off, `552 5.2.2`, a
permanent failure the MTA bounces to the sender; on, `452 4.2.2`, a
temporary failure the MTA keeps queued and retries.


---

## Recipient rate limiting

Caps how many messages one sender may deliver to one recipient inside a moving
window. Beyond the cap that recipient is refused with `451 4.7.0 Rate limit
exceeded for recipient`, and the sender retries later. Nothing is lost and
nothing is bounced. The connection stays open, and the other recipients of the
same transaction are answered as usual.

Counters live in `yarilo-locks`, so the limit is **cluster-wide** — a sender
does not get a fresh allowance by reaching a different backend pod. The key is
the pair (sender IP, recipient mailbox), so one noisy sender cannot exhaust
another's allowance, and one busy mailbox does not throttle its neighbours.

### `rate_limit_enabled`

- Default: `true`
- Type: boolean
- Also accepted as: `enabled`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.rate_limit.enabled`

Gates the whole check.

### `rate_limit_per_recipient_burst`

- Default: `100`
- Type: integer
- Also accepted as: `per_recipient_burst`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.rate_limit.per_recipient_burst`
- See also: `rate_limit_per_recipient_window_seconds`

Messages allowed per sender IP and recipient inside one window.

### `rate_limit_per_recipient_window_seconds`

- Default: `60`
- Type: integer, seconds
- Also accepted as: `per_recipient_window_seconds`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.rate_limit.per_recipient_window_seconds`
- See also: `rate_limit_per_recipient_burst`

Width of the window.


```yaml
protocol:
  lmtp:
    rate_limit:
      rate_limit_enabled: true
      rate_limit_per_recipient_burst: 100
      rate_limit_per_recipient_window_seconds: 60
```

In the Helm chart the same settings live under `protocol.lmtp.rate_limit`
without the prefix (`enabled`, `per_recipient_burst`,
`per_recipient_window_seconds`).

**When to raise it.** The defaults suit ordinary mail and do not suit bulk
delivery into a single account — a migration, a load test, a mailing-list
expansion landing in one mailbox. Those are what the burst and the window are
for. Turning the check off entirely leaves nothing between a misbehaving sender
and a mailbox.

If a lock-service call fails, the delivery is **accepted**: the availability of
the rate limiter is never allowed to block legitimate mail.

---

## Original recipient (ORCPT)

A relay may name a recipient's original address with the `ORCPT` parameter of `RCPT TO` (RFC 3461). yarilo-lmtp-login takes it and passes it on to the backend, which takes it too, without either of them offering DSN. Sieve's vacation uses it as one of the user's addresses when `sieve_vacation_use_original_recipient` is on; see [Sieve](/features/sieve#vacation-replies).

::: warning Postfix sends no ORCPT here
Postfix adds `ORCPT` only for a server that announces DSN, and yarilo does not announce DSN: that would make it responsible for delivery notifications (RFC 3461), which it does not send. So with Postfix in front, no ORCPT arrives and `sieve_vacation_use_original_recipient` has no effect. It takes effect with a relay that sends ORCPT without DSN, such as another IMAP server's LMTP proxy placed in front of yarilo during a migration.
:::

## Delivered-To header

### `lmtp_hdr_delivery_address`

- Default: `final`
- Type: string
- Values: `none` `final` `original`
- Also accepted as: `hdr_delivery_address`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.hdr_delivery_address`

What the `Delivered-To:` header carries; the values are described below.


The values:

| Value | Behaviour |
|:---|:---|
| `none` | No `Delivered-To:` header is added. |
| `final` | `Delivered-To:` shows the address after subaddress stripping (`alice@example.com`). Default. |
| `original` | `Delivered-To:` shows the RCPT TO address as received (`alice+tag@example.com`). |

---

## Client workarounds

### `lmtp_client_workarounds`

- Default: `[]`
- Type: list
- Also accepted as: `client_workarounds`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.client_workarounds`

Compatibility shims for MTA clients that break the protocol; the names
are described below. Unknown names are ignored.


The names:

| Name | Effect |
|:---|:---|
| `whitespace-before-path` | Allows whitespace between the command verb and `<path>`: `MAIL FROM: <user@example.com>`. |
| `mailbox-for-path` | Allows a bare mailbox name without a domain in RCPT TO: `RCPT TO:<alice>`. |

```yaml
protocol:
  lmtp:
    lmtp_client_workarounds:
      - whitespace-before-path
      - mailbox-for-path
```

---

## `protocol.lmtp.proxy`

`yarilo-lmtp-login` reads this section. For each recipient it opens one connection to the backend that the director's LOOKUP names (or to `backend_addr` in standalone mode). Deliveries to different backends run in parallel, and the per-recipient status codes are merged before the reply to the MTA. The backend, `yarilo-lmtp`, ignores the section.

### `lmtp_proxy_timeout`

- Default: `125`
- Type: integer, seconds
- Also accepted as: `timeout`
- Helm: `protocol.lmtp.proxy.lmtp_proxy_timeout`

Cap on one backend delivery: the connect, the LMTP transaction and the
body together. Past it the recipient gets `451 4.2.0` and the MTA
retries. A recipient's userdb field `proxy_timeout` replaces it for that
recipient.


```yaml
protocol:
  lmtp:
    proxy:
      lmtp_proxy_timeout: 60
```

A recipient's userdb field `proxy_timeout` replaces it for that recipient; see [AUTH](/auth/) for the format. When that lookup fails the recipient gets `451 4.3.0 Temporary user lookup failure`; when the value cannot be read, `550 5.3.5 Internal user lookup failure`. A user the userdb does not know is delivered with the global value.

---

## Listener (service-level settings)

```yaml
services:
  lmtp:
    enabled: true
    port: 24
    ssl_mode: no    # no | starttls | ssl
```

The real client IP and recipient identity are carried in the YARILO preamble from `yarilo-lmtp-login`; no HAProxy or XCLIENT handling on the backend.

---

## Example: backend node (yarilo-lmtp)

```yaml
services:
  lmtp:
    enabled: true
    port: 24
    ssl_mode: no

protocol:
  lmtp:
    lmtp_add_received_header: true
    lmtp_hdr_delivery_address: final
    lmtp_user_concurrency_limit: 5
    read_timeout: 300
    write_timeout: 300
```

The backend listens only for preamble connections from `yarilo-lmtp-login`. MTAs connect to `yarilo-lmtp-login`, not directly to this port.

## `lmtp_login_service`

Configuration for `yarilo-lmtp-login`. Set either `backend_addr` (standalone) or `director_addr` (director mode). When both are set, `backend_addr` wins and the service logs a warning at start.

### `backend_addr`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `components.lmtpLogin.backend_addr`
- See also: `director_addr`

Fixed address of the yarilo-lmtp backend, for standalone mode. When both
this and `director_addr` are set, this wins and a warning is logged at
start.

### `director_addr`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `components.lmtpLogin.director_addr`
- See also: `backend_addr`

Address of yarilo-director (`:9102`) for the per-recipient `LOOKUP`.

### `director_tag`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `components.lmtpLogin.director_tag`

Tag pool for the `LOOKUP`. Empty selects the untagged pool; there is no
full-ring mode. A per-user `director_tag` from the userdb overrides it.

### `backend_port`

- Default: `0`
- Type: integer
- Helm: `components.lmtpLogin.backend_port`

Port that replaces the one in the `LOOKUP` result. `0` uses the result
as it is.


**Standalone mode:**

```yaml
lmtp_login_service:
  backend_addr: "yarilo-lmtp.yarilo.svc.cluster.local:24"
```

```yaml
components:
  lmtpLogin:
    enabled: true
    backend_addr: "yarilo-lmtp.yarilo.svc.cluster.local:24"
```

**Director mode:**

```yaml
lmtp_login_service:
  director_addr: "yarilo-director.yarilo.svc.cluster.local:9102"
  director_tag: "prod"
  backend_port: 10024
```

```yaml
components:
  lmtpLogin:
    enabled: true
    director_addr: "yarilo-director.yarilo.svc.cluster.local:9102"
    director_tag: "prod"
    backend_port: 10024
```

Postfix `main.cf`:

```
mailbox_transport = lmtp:inet:[yarilo-lmtp-login.yarilo.svc.cluster.local]:24
```

---
description: "POP3 configuration for yarilo: RFC 1939 with STLS, UIDL, CAPA and XCLIENT, listener ports, TLS modes and the protocol-level settings behind them."
---

# POP3 configuration

Yarilo implements POP3 (RFC 1939) with STLS (RFC 2595), UIDL, CAPA, and XCLIENT.

Listeners: `services.pop3s` (implicit TLS, port 995) and `services.pop3` (STARTTLS, port 110).
See [Services configuration](/architecture/services) for listener-level settings (port, ssl_mode, haproxy_protocol, etc.).

---

## `protocol.pop3`

Protocol-level behaviour, shared across both POP3 listeners.

### `pop3_no_flag_updates`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_no_flag_updates`

`false` sets `\Seen` on retrieved messages at QUIT. `true` changes no
flags on retrieval.

### `pop3_reuse_xuidl`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_reuse_xuidl`

Use the `X-UIDL` message header as the UIDL value. Lets mail migrated
from Courier, qmail or cPanel keep its UIDLs.

### `pop3_uidl_format`

- Default: `%u.%v`
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_uidl_format`

UIDL format string; the variables are listed below.

### `pop3_uidl_duplicates`

- Default: `rename`
- Type: string
- Values: `allow` `rename`
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_uidl_duplicates`

`allow` sends duplicate UIDLs as they are. `rename` appends a `-N`
suffix so every UIDL is unique.

### `pop3_enable_last`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_enable_last`

Advertise and handle the `LAST` command (RFC 1460).

### `pop3_delete_type`

- Default: `expunge`
- Type: string
- Values: `expunge` `flag`
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_delete_type`
- See also: `pop3_deleted_flag`

`expunge` removes a deleted message from disk at QUIT. `flag` sets
`pop3_deleted_flag` instead, so the message stays visible over IMAP.

### `pop3_deleted_flag`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_deleted_flag`

IMAP flag set when `pop3_delete_type` is `flag`, for example
`$POP3Deleted`.

### `pop3_save_uidl`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_save_uidl`

Persist computed UIDLs to a `pop3.uidl` file next to the folder's index.
Later sessions load them, so UIDLs stay the same across index rebuilds
and backend changes.

### `pop3_lock_session`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.pop3.pop3_lock_session`

Create a dotlock at `$HOME/yarilo-pop3-session.lock` after login, so
another replica on the same PVC cannot serve the user at the same time.
Locks older than 10 minutes are stolen.


### `pop3_uidl_format` variables

| Variable | Description |
|:---|:---|
| `%u` | Message UID. |
| `%v` | Mailbox UIDValidity. |
| `%f` | Filename (Maildir only). |
| `%g` | GUID (128-bit hex, dbox/mdbox). |
| `%m` | MD5 of the filename. |

Common presets:

| Format | Result example | Compatible with |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `%u.%v` | `1234.5678` | yarilo default |
| `%08Xu%08Xv` | `000004D2000016C2` | the reference |
| `%f` | `1700000000.M123P456.host:2,S` | Courier (Maildir) |

---

## Soft-delete (flag mode)

When `pop3_delete_type: flag`, messages deleted by a POP3 client are not removed from disk. Instead the flag defined by `pop3_deleted_flag` is set, and the message remains visible in IMAP. This allows users to switch between POP3 and IMAP without losing mail.

```yaml
protocol:
  pop3:
    pop3_delete_type: flag
    pop3_deleted_flag: "$POP3Deleted"
```

---

## Migration from other servers

To migrate users from Courier, qmail, or cPanel without changing UIDL values (which would cause POP3 clients to re-download all mail):

```yaml
protocol:
  pop3:
    pop3_reuse_xuidl: true
    pop3_uidl_format: "%f"      # match the source server's format
    pop3_uidl_duplicates: rename
```

---

## UIDL stability (`pop3_save_uidl`)

By default, UIDLs are computed fresh each session from `pop3_uidl_format`. If the index is rebuilt or a backend migration changes filenames, UIDLs may change — causing POP3 clients to re-download mail they already have.

Enable `pop3_save_uidl` to persist the computed UIDL for each message:

```yaml
protocol:
  pop3:
    pop3_save_uidl: true
```

UIDLs are saved to a `pop3.uidl` file next to the folder's `yarilo.index`, in the index directory (one `uid\tuidl` pair per line) at the end of each session via atomic write. On the next session, saved values are loaded and used for existing UIDs; new messages get fresh UIDLs that are then persisted.

Priority when multiple sources exist: `pop3_reuse_xuidl` header → saved index entry → format-computed value.

---

## Session locking (`pop3_lock_session`)

In multi-replica deployments (yarilo-pop3 `replicas > 1` on a shared PVC), two pods could serve the same user simultaneously — one via POP3 and one via IMAP. Enable `pop3_lock_session` to prevent this:

```yaml
protocol:
  pop3:
    pop3_lock_session: true
```

After login, the session creates `$HOME/yarilo-pop3-session.lock`. A second session for the same user on any pod that shares the filesystem will be rejected with `-ERR mailbox already in use`. The lock is released when the session ends (QUIT or disconnect). Locks older than the session idle timeout, 10 minutes, are automatically treated as stale and stolen.

---

<!-- source: https://doc.yarilomail.org/main/protocols/submission.html -->

# Submission configuration

Yarilo runs two submission listeners. MX inbound (port 25) is handled by an external MTA (Postfix, Exim, etc.) which delivers to yarilo via LMTP (port 24).

| Service key | Port | Role |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `submission` | `587` | Outbound submission — AUTH required, STARTTLS. |
| `submissions` | `465` | Outbound submission — AUTH required, implicit TLS. |

See [Services configuration](/architecture/services) for listener-level settings (`port`, `ssl_mode`, `haproxy_protocol`, `auth_allow_cleartext`).

---

## `protocol.submission`

Protocol-level behaviour shared across both submission listeners.

### `hostname`

- Default: the top-level `hostname`
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.submission.hostname`

EHLO/HELO banner and `Message-ID` domain **for submission only**. Unset
means the installation's name; see [General](/installation/general).
Setting it here does not rename the LMTP banner, the `Received:` header
or a delivered message's `Message-ID`.

### `submission_max_mail_size`

- Default: `40M`
- Type: string
- Also accepted as: `max_message_size`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.max_message_size`

Maximum accepted message size. Takes a size with a unit (`40M`) or bytes.

### `max_line_length`

- Default: `4096`
- Type: integer, bytes
- Helm: `protocol.submission.max_line_length`

Maximum SMTP command or DATA line length.

### `submission_max_recipients`

- Default: `0`
- Type: integer
- Also accepted as: `max_recipients`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.max_recipients`

Maximum recipients per message. `0` is unlimited.

### `recipient_delimiter`

- Default: `+`
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.submission.recipient_delimiter`

Subaddress separator: `user+tag@domain` → `user@domain`. Empty disables
it.

### `submission_client_workarounds`

- Default: `[]`
- Type: list
- Values: `whitespace-before-path` `mailbox-for-path`
- Also accepted as: `client_workarounds`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.client_workarounds`
- See also: `lmtp_client_workarounds`

Compatibility shims for clients that break the protocol. They do the same
as the [LMTP workarounds](/protocols/lmtp#protocol.lmtp.lmtp_client_workarounds)
of the same name.

### `submission_add_received_header`

- Default: `true`
- Type: boolean
- Helm: `protocol.submission.add_received_header`

Prepend a `Received:` trace header to messages before forwarding. Set it
to `false` to keep the sender's address out of the message.


```yaml
protocol:
  submission:
    hostname: mail.example.com
    submission_max_mail_size: 40M
    max_line_length: 4096
    submission_max_recipients: 100
    recipient_delimiter: "+"
    submission_add_received_header: true
```

---

## Submission (port 587 / 465)

Accepts mail from MUAs. AUTH is required. `yarilo-submission-login` offers `PLAIN` and `LOGIN`, plus whatever `yarilo-auth` runs: the SCRAM mechanisms its passdbs can verify (`-PLUS` only over TLS 1.3) and, with OAuth2 configured, `OAUTHBEARER` and `XOAUTH2` (see [OAuth 2.0](/auth/oauth2)). A refused login answers `535`; a mechanism not offered answers `504`. After successful authentication and DATA, the message is forwarded to the configured upstream MTA via `protocol.submission.relay`. If `submission_relay_host` is empty, submission returns `451`.

`auth_allow_cleartext: false` in the service config blocks AUTH on unencrypted connections; pair it with `ssl_mode: starttls` (port 587) or `ssl_mode: ssl` (port 465).

### A proxy in front

A proxy or relay that passes the client's address with XCLIENT needs `xclient_protocol: true` on the listener and its own network in `general.xclient.trusted_nets`, which is empty by default. Only a peer in that list sees `250-XCLIENT` in the EHLO reply and has its forwarded address applied; any other client is not told about XCLIENT. See [General settings](/installation/general#general-xclient).

---

## Relay (`protocol.submission.relay`)

Configures the upstream MTA for submission. One TCP connection per message; any transport error returns `451 4.4.0` to the MUA.

### `submission_relay_host`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Also accepted as: `host`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.host`

Upstream MTA hostname or IP. Empty disables the relay, and submission
answers `451`.

### `submission_relay_port`

- Default: `25`
- Type: integer
- Also accepted as: `port`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.port`

Upstream MTA port.

### `submission_relay_user`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Also accepted as: `user`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.user`

SASL PLAIN username sent to the upstream; `%u` (or `%{user}`) is the
session's user. Empty, with no master, sends no AUTH.

### `submission_relay_master_user`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.master_user`

Log in as this master acting for `submission_relay_user` (the SASL
authzid), or for the session's user when that is empty.

### `submission_relay_password`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Also accepted as: `password`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.password`

SASL PLAIN password, the master's when one is set. Supports
`${ENV_VAR}`. In the chart, `relay.password_secret_ref` takes it from a
Secret instead.

### `submission_relay_ssl`

- Default: `no`
- Type: string
- Values: `no` `starttls` `smtps`
- Also accepted as: `ssl`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.ssl`

Transport security to the upstream.

### `submission_relay_ssl_verify`

- Default: `true`
- Type: boolean
- Also accepted as: `ssl_verify`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.ssl_verify`

Verify the upstream's TLS certificate.

### `submission_relay_ssl_ca`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.ssl_ca`

PEM file the upstream certificate is verified against. Empty means the
system roots.

### `submission_relay_trusted`

- Default: `false`
- Type: boolean
- Also accepted as: `trusted`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.trusted`

Send XCLIENT to the upstream with the client's real IP. The upstream
must advertise XCLIENT.

### `submission_relay_connect_timeout`

- Default: `30`
- Type: integer, seconds
- Also accepted as: `connect_timeout`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.connect_timeout`

TCP connect timeout.

### `submission_relay_command_timeout`

- Default: `300`
- Type: integer, seconds
- Also accepted as: `command_timeout`
- Helm: `protocol.submission.relay.command_timeout`

Per-command timeout.


```yaml
protocol:
  submission:
    relay:
      submission_relay_host: smtp.example.com
      submission_relay_port: 587
      submission_relay_user: relay-user
      submission_relay_password: "${RELAY_PASSWORD}"
      submission_relay_ssl: starttls
      submission_relay_ssl_verify: true
      submission_relay_trusted: false
      submission_relay_connect_timeout: 30
      submission_relay_command_timeout: 300
```

### Telling the relay who sends

A relay that authenticates through yarilo, such as Postfix with `smtpd_sasl_type = dovecot` pointed at `yarilo-sasl-login`, can check the sender against the login (`reject_authenticated_sender_login_mismatch`). For that it must see the user, not a service account. Log in as a master acting for each user:

```yaml
protocol:
  submission:
    relay:
      submission_relay_host: relay.example.internal
      submission_relay_port: 587
      submission_relay_ssl: starttls
      submission_relay_user: "%u"
      submission_relay_master_user: relay-master
      submission_relay_password: "${YARILO_SUBMISSION_RELAY_PASSWORD}"
```

- `relay-master` must be a master user in yarilo-auth (see [Master users](/auth/master_users)).
- The session's user is the one it logged in as, by every mechanism: PLAIN, LOGIN, SCRAM, OAUTHBEARER and XOAUTH2.
- When the relay needs a user (`%u`, or a master with no relay user) and the session has none, the message is refused before the relay is dialled.

A relay login that fails, or cannot be made for want of a user, answers the client `451 4.7.0 Temporary authentication failure, try again later`. The reason is logged with the session id.

In the Helm chart, `relay.password_secret_ref` (`name`, `key`) gives the password from a Secret to every container that relays, as `YARILO_SUBMISSION_RELAY_PASSWORD`.

### JMAP

JMAP `EmailSubmission` sends through this same relay, with the same login as the user and the same limits; see [JMAP](/protocols/jmap#sending-mail).

### Verifying the relay

A relay inside the cluster usually holds a certificate from an internal CA. To verify it against that CA, set `submission_relay_ssl_ca` to the CA's PEM and keep `submission_relay_ssl_verify: true`. With `internal_tls` on, the chart already mounts the internal CA at `/etc/yarilo/internal-tls/ca.crt`.

::: warning
2.4.3 and earlier delivered a reply a step behind after AUTH through the login, so a client could not send through Submission.
:::

The pre-beta short names — `host`, `port`, `user`, `password`, `ssl`, `ssl_verify`, `trusted`, `connect_timeout`, `command_timeout` — are still accepted.

---

<!-- source: https://doc.yarilomail.org/main/reference/rfcs.html -->

---
description: "The RFCs yarilo implements, by service: IMAP, POP3, Submission, LMTP, JMAP, Sieve and ManageSieve, authentication, message format and the policy server, each with its state."
---

# RFC support

The standards each yarilo service implements, and how far. A row is **yes** only when the code serves it and, for an extension a client discovers, the server advertises it: a command a client is never told about is, to that client, absent.

| | meaning |
|:---|:---|
| **yes** | implemented and advertised where the protocol advertises |
| **partial** | usable with the limit given in the note |
| **no** | not implemented; listed because clients or other servers commonly use it |

Drafts and vendor protocols that yarilo also speaks are listed at the end of each section, without a number. [Feature coverage](/architecture/parity) is the same picture by feature rather than by standard.

## IMAP

## Submission

Served by `yarilo-submission`, through `yarilo-submission-login`, which answers `EHLO` until the client has authenticated. The client keeps that answer for the session, so it lists the extensions `yarilo-submission` serves, with the same limits.

| [8314](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8314) | Implicit TLS | yes | port 465 |
| [4954](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4954) | AUTH | yes | |
| [6152](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6152) | 8BITMIME | yes | |
| [1870](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1870) | SIZE | yes | the `submission_max_mail_size` limit |
| [2920](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2920) | PIPELINING | yes | |
| [2034](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2034) | ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES | yes | |
| [3030](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3030) | CHUNKING | yes | |

## JMAP

Served by `yarilo-jmap`, through `yarilo-jmap-login`.

| RFC | Title | State | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [8620](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8620) | JMAP core | yes | session, request envelope, back-references, blob upload and download |
| [8620 §7.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8620#section-7.3) | Push over EventSource | yes | a write on any pod reaches the stream as a `yarilo-locks` event; off with `jmap_push_poll: 0`, see [Push](/protocols/jmap#push) |
| [8621](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8621) | JMAP for Mail | yes | `Mailbox/queryChanges` and `Email/queryChanges` answer `cannotCalculateChanges`, which the RFC allows |
| [8621 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8621#section-7) | Submission | yes | when a relay is configured; identities are read-only |
| [8621 §8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8621#section-8) | Vacation response | yes | with Sieve vacation on |
| [9425](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9425) | JMAP for Quotas | yes | read-only |
| [9661](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9661) | JMAP for Sieve scripts | yes | |
| [8620 §7.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8620#section-7.2) | PushSubscription | no | not built until a client needs push while it is offline; an open EventSource or WebSocket gets every change |
| [8887](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8887) | JMAP over WebSocket | yes | with push; `pushState` resumes on any backend. See [WebSocket](/protocols/jmap#websocket) |

See [JMAP](/protocols/jmap#capabilities).

## Sieve and ManageSieve

Scripts run at delivery; `sieve_extensions` narrows the set a deployment offers.

| RFC | Title | State | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [5804](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5804) | ManageSieve | yes | |
| [5228](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5228) | Sieve | yes | `fileinto`, `reject`, `envelope`, `encoded-character` |
| [3894](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3894) | `copy` | yes | |
| [5173](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5173) | `body` | yes | |
| [5183](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5183) | `environment` | yes | |
| [5229](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5229) | `variables` | yes | |
| [5230](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5230) | `vacation` | yes | |
| [5231](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5231) | `relational` | yes | |
| [5232](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5232) | `imap4flags` | yes | |
| [5233](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5233) | `subaddress` | yes | |
| [5235](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5235) | `spamtest`, `spamtestplus`, `virustest` | yes | report "not scanned" until a status header is configured |
| [5260](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5260) | `date`, `index` | yes | |
| [5293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5293) | `editheader` | yes | |
| [5429](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5429) | `ereject` | yes | |
| [5435](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5435) | `enotify` | yes | |
| [5436](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5436) | `mailto` notification method | yes | |
| [5463](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5463) | `ihave` | yes | |
| [5490](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5490) | `mailbox`, `mboxmetadata`, `servermetadata` | yes | |
| [5703](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5703) | `foreverypart`, `mime`, `extracttext`, `replace`, `enclose` | yes | |
| [6131](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6131) | `vacation-seconds` | yes | |
| [6609](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6609) | `include` | yes | |
| [6785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6785) | IMAP events (`imapsieve`) | yes | |
| [7352](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7352) | `duplicate` | yes | |
| [8579](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8579) | `special-use` | yes | |
| [8580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8580) | `fcc` | yes | |
| [9042](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9042) | `mailboxid` | yes | |

Also implemented: `regex` (draft), and the `vnd.yarilo.*` extensions. See [Sieve](/features/sieve).

## Authentication

SASL mechanisms run in `yarilo-auth` and are offered by every protocol that authenticates.

| RFC | Title | State | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [4422](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4422) | SASL | yes | |
| [4616](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4616) | PLAIN | yes | |
| [5802](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5802) | SCRAM-SHA-1, SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS | yes | |
| [7677](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7677) | SCRAM-SHA-256, SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS | yes | |
| [9266](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9266) | `tls-exporter` channel binding | yes | the `-PLUS` mechanisms, over TLS 1.3 |
| [7628](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7628) | OAUTHBEARER | yes | with an OAuth2 passdb |
| [7662](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662) | Token introspection | yes | |
| [7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519) | JWT | yes | `local` mode |
| [6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) | OAuth 2.0 password grant | yes | for PLAIN and LOGIN, with `oauth2_grant_url` |
| [2195](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2195) | CRAM-MD5 | no | |
| [2831](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2831) | DIGEST-MD5 | no | |
| [4752](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4752) | GSSAPI (Kerberos) | no | |
| [4422 App. A](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4422#appendix-A) | EXTERNAL | no | |

Also implemented: `LOGIN` (draft) and `XOAUTH2` (Google). See [SCRAM](/auth/scram) and [OAuth 2.0](/auth/oauth2).

## Message format and transport

| RFC | Title | State | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322) | Internet Message Format | yes | |
| [2045](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2045)–[2049](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2049) | MIME | yes | |
| [2231](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2231) | MIME parameter continuations | yes | parameters keep their order and spelling |
| [8446](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446) | TLS 1.3 | yes | TLS 1.2 is the default minimum |
| [6066](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6066) | TLS `server_name` (SNI) | partial | the name picks between `ssl_server_cert_file` and `ssl_server_alt_cert_file`, by the names each covers; there are no certificates per name. The policy server gets it as `%{local_name}` |

Also spoken: the HAProxy PROXY protocol on any listener with `haproxy_protocol`, and the Postfix policy delegation protocol in `yarilo-quota-status`. Behind a PROXY header, the client it names is the connection's remote address, and the proxy itself is what the policy server gets as `%{real_remote_ip}` and `%{real_remote_port}`.

## Policy server

`yarilo-auth` calls an HTTP [policy server](/auth/policy) before and after each login.

| RFC | Title | State | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110) | HTTP semantics | yes | `POST`, over HTTP/1.1 or, through TLS, HTTP/2 |
| [8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259) | JSON | yes | the request body and the answer |
| [7617](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617) | Basic authentication | partial | `auth_policy_server_api_header` is sent as written, so `Authorization: Basic …` works; yarilo does not encode it |
| [9562](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562) | UUID | yes | version 4, from `%{generate:uuid}` in a request template |
| [4648](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648) | Base64, base64url and base16 | yes | the `base64` and `unbase64` template filters, `url=1` for the URL alphabet and `pad=0` without padding; `hexlify` and `unhexlify` for base16 |

---

<!-- source: https://doc.yarilomail.org/main/storage/dict.html -->

# Dictionaries

`pkg/dict` is the general key-value store every yarilo feature that needs
durable per-user or per-mailbox state sits on top of. A single contract
(`Dict` + `Tx` + `Iterator`) is satisfied by multiple drivers; the
choice of driver (`file`, `redis`, `sql`, `memory`, `fail`) is made via
YAML config, not code. The drivers run in the `yarilo-dict` service
(mTLS, port 9107); a session binary names a dict and reaches it through
`pkg/dict/proxy`, and needs `dict_service.dict_addr` set to start — see
[The dict service](#the-dict-service).

See [Architecture §Dict abstraction](/architecture/#dict-abstraction)
for the design rationale; this document is the operator reference for
configuring and operating dicts.

---

## Concepts

| Term | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| **Dict** | A named key-value store instance, declared once in `yarilo.yaml` under `dicts:` |
| **Driver** | The backing implementation (`file`, `redis`, `sql`, `memory`, `fail`) |
| **Settings** | Driver-specific configuration map (path / addr / dsn / ...) |
| **Namespace** | `priv/` (per-user) and `shared/` (per-resource) key prefixes — application convention; not enforced by drivers |
| **OpSettings** | Per-call context: username, home dir, TTL — passed by callers, used by drivers; through the dict service the TTL travels with the transaction |

## YAML schema

```yaml
dicts:
  <name>:
    driver: file|redis|sql|memory|fail
    settings:
      # driver-specific (see below)
    expire_secs: 0          # default TTL for writes (drivers with TTL support)
    username: ""            # default OpSettings.Username
    home_dir: ""            # default OpSettings.HomeDir
```

`<name>` is the logical identifier yarilo features look up
(e.g. `metadata`, `quota_count`, `acl`). Multiple named dicts may share
one backing service through different prefixes/namespaces.

## The dict service

`yarilo-dict` opens the `redis` and `sql` dicts and serves them over internal
mTLS; the session processes link no engine and reach it by name. The `file`
driver is the exception: the process that uses it opens it itself (see
[file](#file)).

```yaml
dict_service:
  dict_listen: ":9107"     # yarilo-dict: where it serves
  dict_addr: "yarilo-dict:9107"   # every other process: where to find it
  dict_max_conns: 8
```

### `dict_listen`

- Default: none
- Type: string
- Helm: `components.dict.listen`

Listen address of `yarilo-dict`. Required: the service exits at startup
without it.

### `dict_addr`

- Default: none
- Type: string

`host:port` of `yarilo-dict`, read by session processes. Required as
soon as a `redis` or `sql` dict is configured; empty with only `file`
dicts is fine. The chart derives it from the release's `yarilo-dict`
Service.

### `dict_max_conns`

- Default: `8`
- Type: integer
- Helm: `components.dict.max_conns`

Connections one session process keeps to one named dict. An iteration
holds its connection until it ends, so `1` makes every other operation
on that dict wait behind it.


The chart renders all three from `components.dict` (`enabled`, `listen`,
default `:9107`, `max_conns`, default `8`) and derives `dict_addr` from the
release's own `yarilo-dict` Service, so the port cannot disagree between the
listener and the clients.

---

## Drivers

### file

JSON file. Atomic temp-file + rename on every commit.

The path is a template expanded **per operation** from the operation's
user (`%u`, `%h`, `%n`, `%d`, `%i`), so one configured dict gives every
user a file of their own. A path naming `%h` is refused on any operation
that carries no home, rather than resolving to a path shared by everyone.

Safe across processes: a commit takes a lock on `<path>.lock`, re-reads
the document under the lock and then rewrites it, so two pods writing the
same user's file keep each other's keys. Reads take no lock — they stat
the file and reload when its stamp has moved.

Unlike `redis` and `sql`, this driver is opened by the process that uses
it, not by `yarilo-dict`: it links no engine. It is the default for
annotations.

```yaml
dicts:
  metadata:
    driver: file
    settings:
      path: "%h/yarilo-metadata.json"
      lock_method: ""          # flock (default), fcntl or dotlock
```

Settings:

| Key | Type | Required | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `path` | string | yes | Filesystem path; `%u`/`%h`/`%n`/`%d`/`%i` are expanded per operation |
| `lock_method` | string | no | Write lock transport: `flock` (default), `fcntl`, `dotlock`. Match the mail volume's `storage_lock_method` |

### memory

In-process `map[string]row`. Lost on process exit. For unit tests and
short-lived dev runs.

```yaml
dicts:
  scratch:
    driver: memory
```

No settings.

### fail

Every operation returns `ErrFailDriver`. Used in code paths that need a
non-nil `dict.Dict` even when the feature is disabled.

```yaml
dicts:
  disabled-metadata:
    driver: fail
    settings:
      message: "metadata feature disabled by admin"   # optional
```

### redis

Production cluster backend. SET/GET/DEL, MULTI/EXEC for transactions,
INCRBY for atomic counters, EXPIRE for TTL, SCAN for iteration. One
Redis string per dict key. Prefix-isolated so multiple named dicts can
share one Redis instance.

```yaml
dicts:
  metadata:
    driver: redis
    settings:
      addr: "yarilo-redis.yarilo.svc.cluster.local:6379"
      password: ""                # optional AUTH
      db: 0                       # logical database
      prefix: "yarilo:metadata:"  # prepended to every key on the wire
      dial_timeout: "5s"          # Go duration string
    expire_secs: 86400            # default TTL: 1 day
```

Settings:

| Key | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `addr` | string | yes | — | `host:port` |
| `password` | string | no | `""` | AUTH; empty = no auth |
| `db` | int | no | `0` | Logical database |
| `prefix` | string | no | `""` | Per-dict key prefix, taken literally. A `%`-variable is refused at startup: the dict opens once per process, so nothing would expand it, and a per-user key already carries `priv/<user>/` |
| `dial_timeout` | string | no | `5s` | Go duration |

### sql

Production cluster backend. PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite via `database/sql`.
One row per dict key. Auto-creates the table on first Open. Per-namespace
to allow multiple dicts in one schema. See **Mapped mode** below for a
column-per-key layout (quota_clone).

```yaml
dicts:
  metadata:
    driver: sql
    settings:
      driver: postgres            # | mysql | sqlite
      dsn: "postgres://yarilo:secret@pg.yarilo.svc:5432/yarilo?sslmode=disable"
      table: "dict_kv"            # default
      namespace: "metadata"       # per-dict namespace within the table
```

Settings:

| Key | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `driver` | string | yes | — | `sqlite`, `postgres` or `mysql` |
| `dsn` | string | yes | — | `database/sql` DSN |
| `table` | string | no | `dict_kv` | Table name; must match `[A-Za-z0-9_]+` (generic mode) |
| `namespace` | string | no | `""` | Per-dict key prefix within the shared table (generic mode) |
| `maps` | list | no | — | Column bindings; presence enables **mapped mode** (see below) |
| `max_open_conns` | int | no | mysql `25`, postgres `8`, sqlite `1` | Connections the dict's pool may hold, in use and idle; `0` = unlimited |
| `max_idle_conns` | int | no | = `max_open_conns` | Idle connections kept for reuse; `0` keeps none |
| `conn_max_lifetime` | int | no | `300` | Seconds before a connection is recycled, so it does not stay pinned to a server that failed over; `0` = never |
| `conn_max_idle_time` | int | no | `60` | Seconds an idle connection is kept before it is closed; `0` = never. A negative value in any of these four fails the dict at open |

Schema (auto-created):

```sql
CREATE TABLE dict_kv (
    namespace TEXT NOT NULL,
    k         TEXT NOT NULL,
    v         BLOB NOT NULL,         -- BYTEA on postgres
    expires   BIGINT,                -- unix seconds; NULL = no TTL
    PRIMARY KEY (namespace, k)
);
CREATE INDEX dict_kv_expires_idx ON dict_kv(expires) WHERE expires IS NOT NULL;
```

`ExpireScan` runs `DELETE FROM dict_kv WHERE namespace = $1 AND expires <= $2`.

#### Mapped mode (column mapping)

By default the sql driver stores every key in the generic `(namespace, k, v)`
layout, so a quota_clone target writes two rows per user. Setting `maps` switches
the dict to **mapped mode**: each key binds to a table **column**, producing a
clean per-user schema an external reader (billing, dashboards) can query
directly. Keys mapped to the same table share one row (the `username_field` is
the primary key), so different columns of the same user coexist.

```yaml
dicts:
  quota_clone_mysql:
    driver: sql
    settings:
      driver: mysql               # sqlite | postgres | mysql
      dsn: "${YARILO_DB_DSN}"
      maps:
        - { key: "priv/quota/storage",  table: quota, username_field: username, value_field: bytes }
        - { key: "priv/quota/messages", table: quota, username_field: username, value_field: messages }
```

The operator owns the table — mapped mode does **not** auto-create it (column
types are the operator's choice):

```sql
CREATE TABLE quota (username VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY, bytes BIGINT, messages BIGINT);
-- one row per user: (u1@d00001.test, 860809, 13)
```

> **Every column other than `username_field` must be nullable (or carry a
> `DEFAULT`).** A `Set` inserts only `(username_field, value_field)`, so the
> first write for a new user leaves sibling columns unset — a `NOT NULL` sibling
> would reject that insert. `Unset` also relies on the column being nullable.

Mapped mode is validated at startup: `New` runs a
`SELECT <value_field> FROM <table> LIMIT 0` for every map, so a typo in a table/column name or a forgotten
`CREATE TABLE` fails at Open rather than silently on the first write. Per-key
TTL (`expire_secs`) and `ExpireScan` are unavailable in mapped mode (mapped
columns carry no expiry) and return an error.

Each map entry:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `key` | yes | Dict key to map (matched exactly) |
| `table` | yes | Target table; must match `[A-Za-z0-9_]+` |
| `username_field` | yes | Column holding the user (primary key); scoped by `OpSettings.Username` |
| `value_field` | yes | Column the key's value is written to / read from |

Behaviour in mapped mode:

- **Set** → single-column upsert keyed on `username_field` (`ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` / `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`).
- **Lookup** → `SELECT <value_field> FROM <table> WHERE <username_field> = ?`; a `NULL` column reads as "not found".
- **Unset** → sets the column to `NULL` (the row is shared by sibling columns and is never deleted).
- **AtomicInc** / **Iterate** → unsupported (error); quota_clone uses only Set.
- A username is required; an unmapped key errors.

---

## Managing dictionaries with yarctl

`yarctl backend dict` is a client of `yarilo-backend-api`, which owns the
configured dicts. The CLI never opens a dict itself: it names one, and the
operation runs in the backend-api process against that dict's driver. A dict
the backend-api configuration does not declare cannot be reached, and there
is no ad-hoc driver mode. How `yarctl` finds and authenticates to the
backend-api is in [yarctl](/operations/yarilo_admin#backend-plane).

Per-op identity, accepted by every command that runs an operation:

| Flag | Maps to |
|:---|:---|
| `--user USER` | `OpSettings.Username` |
| `--home DIR` | `OpSettings.HomeDir` |
| `--expire-secs N` | `OpSettings.ExpireSecs` |

The backend-api does not look a home up from the user: a `file` dict whose
path names `%h` needs `--home` as well as `--user`, or the operation is refused.

### Commands

```sh
yarctl backend dict drivers                                       # drivers registered on backend-api
yarctl backend dict exists NAME                                   # does NAME resolve to a configured dict?

yarctl backend dict lookup [op-flags] NAME KEY                    # print value
yarctl backend dict iterate [op-flags] [--recurse] [--no-value] [--exact] \
                            [--sort-key|--sort-value] NAME PATH   # list rows

yarctl backend dict set [--value-stdin] [op-flags] NAME KEY [VALUE]   # write
yarctl backend dict unset [op-flags] NAME KEY                     # delete
yarctl backend dict atomic-inc [op-flags] NAME KEY DELTA          # integer add (delta may be negative)

yarctl backend dict expire-scan NAME                              # drop TTL-expired rows

yarctl backend dict commit-batch [op-flags] NAME < script.txt     # multi-op atomic transaction
```

`iterate` is streamed from the server, so it is safe over a large prefix. It
prints one `KEY<TAB>VALUE` line per row, or the key alone with `--no-value`.
A value that is not printable text is shown as `base64:…`. Writes print `ok`;
`atomic-inc` on a key that does not exist prints `not-found`.

### `commit-batch` script format

TAB-delimited, one op per line. Empty lines and `#`-prefixed lines are
ignored. Values are base64-encoded so binary content survives.

```
# Initialise per-user quota counters
set	priv/quota/storage	MA==
set	priv/quota/messages	MA==

# Bump storage by 1 KiB (delta is plain text, not base64)
atomic-inc	priv/quota/storage	1024

unset	priv/old/key
```

Pipe the script:

```sh
yarctl backend dict commit-batch --user alice@example.com quota < initialise.dict
```

### Example session

```sh
$ HOME_DIR=/var/mail/example.com/alice@example.com

$ yarctl backend dict set --user alice@example.com --home $HOME_DIR metadata priv/box/INBOX/comment "first message arrived"
ok

$ yarctl backend dict lookup --user alice@example.com --home $HOME_DIR metadata priv/box/INBOX/comment
first message arrived

$ yarctl backend dict iterate --user alice@example.com --home $HOME_DIR --recurse --sort-key metadata priv/
priv/box/INBOX/comment	first message arrived
```

---

## Choosing a driver

| Topology | Recommended driver |
|:---|:---|
| Per-user state on the mail volume (annotations, and the default) | `file`, one file per user under `%h` |
| Standalone single-pod helm release | `file` |
| State that must live off the mail volume, shared by all pods | `redis` (shared Redis Service) |
| Already running Postgres for other yarilo state | `sql` driver, `postgres` mode |
| Unit tests | `memory` |
| "Feature disabled" wiring | `fail` |

The choice is config-only — switching from `file` to `redis` is a
`yarilo.yaml` edit, not a rebuild. What does change with it is who opens
the dict: `file` is opened by the session, an engine by `yarilo-dict`. This is the
**config-not-binary** rule that every yarilo storage decision honours.

---

<!-- source: https://doc.yarilomail.org/main/storage/ -->

# Mailbox storage

Mailbox backends (Maildir, sdbox, mdbox) and the FileIndex (binary mail-index v7.3 wire
format: `.index` / `.index.log` / `.index.names`). All index mutations go through the
cross-process mailbox lock (`yarilo-locks`); sessions sharing a pod serialise on an
in-process `sync.RWMutex` — the Redis lock is only ever contested across pods, not within
a single pod. See also [mdbox Alt Storage (Cold Tiering)](/storage/mdbox_alt).

## Path templates

Every path setting that can differ per user — `mail_home`, `mail_path`,
`mail_inbox_path`, `mail_index_path`, `mail_control_path`, `mail_volatile_path` and
`mail_alt_path` — is a template expanded against the user. Two spellings are
accepted, and nothing else is.

| short form | expression form | expands to |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `%u` | `%{user}` | the full username, `alice@example.com` |
| `%n` | `%{user \| username}` | the local part, `alice` |
| `%d` | `%{user \| domain}` | the domain, `example.com` |
| `%h`, or a leading `~/` | `%{home}` | the user's home directory |
| `%2.256Nu` | `%{user \| sha1 % 256 \| hex(2)}` | a hash bucket, `d5` |
| `%%` | — | a literal `%` |

The expression form is a variable followed by filters: `username`, `domain`, `lower`,
`upper`, `md5`, `sha1`, and `hex(n)`. A hash becomes a number through a modulo
(`sha1 % 256`) and a number becomes text through `hex(n)`, which zero-pads to `n` digits
and keeps the low ones; a negative width pads on the right and keeps the high ones.

**The two forms do not hash the same way, deliberately.** An expression names its
algorithm, so `%{user | sha1 % 256}` is SHA-1 while the older `%2.256Nu` stays MD5. Each
does what it says, and neither changes where an existing deployment's users already live.
The expression form matches the reference implementation byte for byte, including reading
the digest as a big-endian integer from its **last** eight bytes — so a config migrated
from it keeps every user in the bucket they already had.

**A template that cannot be expanded stops startup**, naming the key and the sequence that
was not understood. There is no pass-through: a template copied from a newer reference
config used to produce a directory literally named `%{user | sha1 % 256 | hex(2)}` —
created, written to, and never mentioned.

The same templates are accepted in the matching userdb fields, and expanded the same way
on every path — a delivery and an interactive session resolve one user to one set of
directories. (Before 2.3.133 the delivery path resolved `~/` in `mail_path` /
`mail_inbox_path` but left `%u` alone, so the two could disagree.)

Hash buckets matter once a directory holds one entry per user, as a
`mail_volatile_path` on a local disk does. The chart leaves the key unset; the
example values use the short form:

```yaml
storage:
  mail_volatile_path: "/tmp/yarilo-volatile/%2.256Nu/%u"
```

Switching that to an expression changes the buckets — even
`%{user | md5 % 256 | hex(2)}`, since the short form reads the first four
bytes of the digest and the expression the last eight — so on a running
deployment it moves every user's directory.

## Maildir sync-on-open

**Maildir sync-on-open** (`storage.maildir_sync_on_select`, default `true`): on
SELECT/EXAMINE, STATUS and IDLE the Maildir index is reconciled against `cur/` and `new/`,
so a message delivered by an external MDA or moved/renamed by a second MUA appears without
an operator rebuild — files in `new/` are migrated to `cur/`, new files gain a UID,
vanished files are expunged, and out-of-band flag renames keep their UID. It is gated on a
cheap `cur/`+`new/` mtime token, so a quiescent folder costs a single `stat`. Only Maildir
honours it; dbox stays index-authoritative.

## dbox reactive rebuild

**dbox reactive rebuild** (`storage.dbox_reactive_rebuild`, default `true`): dbox is
index-authoritative and does not scan storage on every access, but it self-heals
reactively. When an **sdbox** read hits a missing or corrupt message file the folder is
flagged (a persisted FSCKD marker in the index header); the next SELECT, STATUS or IDLE
